quiz.problem: Two options can be defended. The right answer's feedback quotes Matt's rule, "you don't need to review every reversible decision", and that rule supports option c ("None") just as well as b. The prompt also says "and the diff agrees", which means the reader has already checked the call. That removes the only reason c's feedback gives against it ("You still check that the call is right").
quiz.evidence: Feedback on b: "Matt's rule: you don't need to review every reversible decision, but you must review every irreversible one." Feedback on c: "Skimming isn't skipping. You still check that the call is right and the Evidence is real." The LlgiOCmFG_w transcript at 22:09-22:15 says reversible decisions don't really need review. The English v1.3 video (BsJGo1wFTvQ 7:01-7:05) says only that you don't need to review a small-blast-radius two-way door "very hard", and that line is the one that actually supports a skim.
quiz.fix:
Replace the block with:
```test scenario-review-effort
A PR changes the wording on one button. Its Merge Danger says "Door: two-way. Blast Radius: small." How much review does it need?
- [ ] A line-by-line read, because every PR deserves equal care.
  > Equal care for everything means too little care for the PRs that can't be undone. Spend it where reversal is hard.
- [x] A quick skim that checks the door call holds.
  > Right. Matt says a small two-way door doesn't need a hard review. The skim is how you confirm the call, because the agent that wrote the code made it.
- [ ] None: a two-way door can be merged unread.
  > The call comes from the agent that wrote the code. A quick look is how you catch a "two-way" that isn't.
- [ ] Block it until the team writes screenshot tests.
  > That's out of proportion for a wording change that a revert undoes.
```

quiz.problem: Two of the three distractors are not real misconceptions: b has the preview before the branch, and d merges before the PR exists. Option a (merge, then test) checks the same point as spot-merge-then-test. The right chain is copied from goal 1, the flow Scene and the Cheat sheet, so the question is recall. It also misses a sequencing rule the Lesson teaches but never tests: review comes before the body (`/code-review`, then `/pr`), and you branch before you build.
quiz.evidence: Right answer: "branch → pull request → preview with its own database → test it → squash and merge → production". Cheat sheet line 329: "Preview → test it → squash and merge → production". Body lines 201-202 teach "Start on a branch" and "Review before the body", and no question tests either.
quiz.fix:
Replace the block with the version below. All four options use the same steps and three are the same length, so there's no length tell. If this id is already in the live database, use a new id.
```test sequence-ship
A small feature for a recipe site set up like this one is ready to build. Which order gets it to production safely?
- [ ] branch → build → `/pr` writes the body → `/code-review` → open the PR → test the preview → squash and merge
  > The body should describe a diff that's already been reviewed, so `/code-review` comes first.
- [ ] branch → build → `/code-review` → open the PR → test the preview → squash and merge → `/pr` writes the body
  > The body is for the reviewer, so it has to exist before anyone reviews or merges the PR.
- [x] branch → build → `/code-review` → `/pr` writes the body → open the PR → test the preview → squash and merge
  > Right. Review, then describe, then test on the copy. The merge is the last step and the only one that touches production.
- [ ] build on `main` → `/code-review` → branch → `/pr` writes the body → open the PR → test the preview → squash and merge
  > `/implement` commits to whatever branch you're on, so building first puts the work on `main`. Branch before you build.
```

quiz.problem: The scenario is Matt's own example (a tiny change that emails a lot of people), and the right answer restates the Lesson's one direct quote ("rolling back a commit won't unsend a batch of emails"), so it's easy to spot by recall. Distractors b and d are straw men: no one thinks only big PRs have doors, or that email features shouldn't go through a PR. The real misconception, that reverting switches the feature off again, isn't offered.
quiz.evidence: Right answer: "A revert can't unsend emails that already went out." Body line 199 quotes "rolling back a commit won't unsend a batch of emails". Option d: "Email features should never ship through a PR."
quiz.fix:
Keep the prompt and option c, and change the others:
- [x] Emails already sent stay sent after a revert.
  > Right. Anything sent out into the world is a one-way door, however small the diff. Read this one slowly.
- [ ] Nothing: reverting turns the weekly email off again.
  > It stops future emails. The ones that already went out can't be pulled back, and that's what makes the door one-way.
- [ ] The call is right; it just needs a wider blast radius.
  > (keep the current feedback)
- [ ] Nothing: a two-line diff is too small to be a one-way door.
  > Size doesn't decide the door. Matt's own one-way example is a tiny change that accidentally emails 60,000 people.
The right answer stays in position a and is the shortest option.

```test scenario-repo-template
Your team's repo already has a `.github/pull_request_template.md`, and you want agent-written bodies to respect it. What do you do?

- [ ] Delete the repo's template so only one is left.
```
